speed_vs_bounce.tracking_check: daily sessions 2026-09-28 to 2026-10-27 (30 rows) never moved more than 1.8 times from one day to the next, so tracking was steady
speed_vs_bounce.pages: 10 of 10 tested pages have 30 or more sessions (8 needed)
speed_vs_bounce.reading: Slower pages bounce more: rank correlation 0.72 across 10 pages. The 2 blog posts are the two slowest pages and also the highest bounce rates, and blog readers often leave after one article whatever the speed. Without them the correlation is 0.45 across 8 pages. This is an association across pages, not proof that speed causes the bounces.
speed_vs_bounce.ga4_vs_search_console: GA4 sessions on the tested pages (25,190, all channels) are 3.4 times their Search Console clicks (7,490), so there is no sign that GA4 undercounts

speed_vs_ad_conversions.pages: 5 landing pages with 100 or more clicks (5 needed), all already tested in this run, so no template was swapped out; /demo/ (85 clicks) is under 100 clicks and left out
speed_vs_ad_conversions.reading: Slower ad landing pages convert worse: rank correlation -0.9 across 5 pages. The two industry pages are the slowest (lab LCP 6.9 s and 6.4 s) and convert at 3.0% of clicks, against 7.9% for the other 3. They take 2,220 of the 4,215 paid clicks and are the second LCP target above. The home and pricing pages also carry brand searches, which convert better whatever the speed, so this is an association, not a measured effect of speed.
